title: What happens during a plane's take-off
examples: How does a plane take off?
How fast does a plane go when it takes off?

explain.say: Take-off is a race to a speed where the wings make more lift than the plane weighs. The pilots set take-off thrust, release the brakes, and the plane accelerates down the runway.

draw.text: What happens during a plane's take-off

explain.say: Before every flight the crew works out a speed called V1. Below V1 they can still stop safely on the runway if something goes wrong; once past V1 they are committed to taking off.
At the rotate speed the pilot gently pulls back, raising the nose. The wing meets the air at a steeper angle, lift grows past the weight, and the wheels leave the ground.
Once climbing safely, the crew raises the landing gear to cut drag, then retracts the flaps as speed builds. A typical airliner lifts off at around 250 to 300 kilometres per hour.

faq.a: V1 is the decision speed for take-off, worked out before each flight. If a serious problem happens before V1 the pilots abort and brake to a stop; after V1 there isn't enough runway left to stop, so they continue.
asks: What does V1 mean when a plane takes off?

faq.a: Rotate is the moment the pilot pulls back on the controls to lift the nose. Tilting the wing to a higher angle makes extra lift, so the plane lifts off a few seconds later.
asks: Why does the nose lift first on take-off?

faq.q: How fast does a plane go when it takes off?
faq.a: Most airliners lift off at about 240 to 330 kilometres per hour, depending on their weight, flap setting, the air temperature and how high the airport is.
asks: How fast is a plane on take-off?

faq.q: Why do planes take off into the wind?
faq.a: Wings care about speed through the air, not over the ground. A headwind gives extra airspeed for free, so the plane lifts off at a lower ground speed and uses less runway.
asks: Does wind help a plane take off?

faq.q: Why are take-offs harder on hot days?
faq.a: Hot air is thinner, so the wings make less lift and the engines less thrust at the same speed. Planes need a longer run, or must carry less weight, at hot or high airports.
asks: Why do planes need longer runways in hot weather?

facts: A headwind shortens the take-off run because the wings need airspeed, not ground speed.
Full take-off thrust is only allowed for a few minutes before the engines are reduced to climb thrust.

quiz.say: A warning light comes on after the plane has passed V1. What do the pilots do?
quiz.show: A problem after V1: the pilots…

options.show: Brake hard to stop on the runway
options.say: Brake hard to stop on the runway

quiz.why: After V1 there is not enough runway left to stop safely, so the crew continues and deals with the problem in the air.

wrong.1: Past V1, braking could run the plane off the end of the runway.
wrong.2: Turning at take-off speed would be very dangerous.
